about: What a host must do when a checking provider breaks a rule that no schema can express. `run` says how the one run ended. `outcome` is `verdict` with the verdict the host records, or `refused` with the reason. Nothing may be recorded as passed except in the control and in the cases whose outcome is the verdict `passed`. `runs` is how many runs the executor must have been given, no more and no fewer. `deadline_ms`, where given, is the deadline the host is given; `names_a_missing_file` makes the obligation name a file that is not among the inputs.

cases.why: A control: a provider that keeps every rule must be accepted, or the other cases prove nothing.
A run that did not exit ends the check in error. The provider is not asked what it thinks.
An executor that cannot be reached is reported as exactly that.
A verdict rests on a run.
A result may not claim more than the manifest declares.
A verdict that states no strength claims one the host cannot bound.
The set of verdicts is closed.
An answer asks for a run or gives a verdict, never both.
An answer that does neither is no answer.
A provider may start only tools it declared.
The same holds for a tool named in an argument.
A program path lies inside the tool it names.
So does a file of a tool named in an argument.
A run starts inside its working directory.
A run writes inside its working directory.
A run may read only what its result is keyed by.
A later run may use only what is in the key.
An answer matches its request.
What a provider says a file contains is never taken on its word.
The same holds for a file it attaches to its verdict: the bytes are hashed again.
An attachment lies inside the working directory.
A check may ask for the same run twice, to see whether a result repeats. Each is submitted under its own key, which includes its number, so the second is never answered from the first.
A tool the manifest declares but the check was not given is not in the key of its result, so a run may not start it.
The same holds for such a tool named in an argument.
A tool named in an argument is a tool named, with or without a file after it.
Every tool named in an argument is looked at, not only the first.
A run uses the tools the check was given, by digest. Another digest is another tool.
The tools a run lists are among those the check was given.
An argument holds no NUL: what follows it would be cut off or read as something else.
A result states the class of strength the manifest declares. A test is not a proof, whatever its rank.
A failure rests on a run as much as a pass does.
The ceiling holds for a failure as for a pass.
An answer carries the id of its request.
The opening echo must come back unchanged, or the two sides do not read text the same way.
A check may ask for eight runs. The ninth is refused before it starts.
A control for the limit: exactly eight runs are allowed.
An argument may not name a file outside the run's own files: an absolute path is refused.
Nor one that climbs out of them.
A run must be given every file its obligation names; a run that reads nothing it was given cannot check anything.
A run must target the platform the check was asked for.
An absolute path inside an option is still outside the run's files.
So is a list of arguments read from another file.
So is a path in a home directory.
So is a URL.
A path glued to a flag is still a path.
So is the parent directory glued to a flag.
A tool file must be the whole argument; anything appended is refused.
A variable can change what a program loads; the stage-0 host allows none.
A run may not write over a file it was given.
A character that only looks like a separator is refused too: a free word may hold printable ASCII only.
An attachment whose bytes have the identity it states is accepted: a host that refuses every attachment would otherwise pass.
A provider may end a check in error after a run; that is a verdict, not a broken rule.
A provider may say at the start that it cannot check this; unsupported needs no run.
A provider that answers a request with an error ends the check; nothing is recorded as a result.
A provider that does not answer within the deadline ends the check.
A run's arguments are a list of strings.
The class of strength must match for failed as for passed.
Two rules broken at once: the platform is checked first, so the reason says so.
Two rules broken at once in a final: attachments are checked before the verdict.
A provider that starts a process of its own: when the check ends, that process must be gone too.
An executor that fails and prints nothing ends the check in error; the provider is not asked to interpret it.
An executor that exits well but prints no report ends the check in error.
A report saying the run executed on another platform than it described is an error, never a result.
A report naming another tool digest than the run described is an error, never a result.
An obligation names a file the check was not given; the check is refused before the provider is sent anything.
